title: LLM serving: tokens, KV cache, GPU memory, why it is slow and expensive
story:
A conventional web request is served in single-digit milliseconds by a process sharing a general-purpose machine with dozens of its neighbours. Serving a large language model is a different kind of activity, and the reason is not that the arithmetic is harder. It is that the weights have to move.

Take the hardware as the reference point. The NVIDIA H100 in its SXM form factor carries 80GB of HBM3 with 3.35TB/s of memory bandwidth, draws up to 700W of configurable thermal design power, and connects over NVLink at 900GB/s. Worth knowing as a fact about procurement rather than about tensors: the SXM part is not sold as a standalone card at all, only as a component of an HGX baseboard carrying four or eight of them inside a partner or vendor system.

Now the derivation that explains everything else. A model generates autoregressively, one token at a time, and each token requires a full forward pass. For a dense model, a forward pass reads every parameter. So consider a seventy-billion-parameter model at sixteen bits, which is two bytes per parameter: a hundred and forty gigabytes must cross the memory bus to produce one token. Divide that by 3.35TB/s and the floor is roughly forty-two milliseconds per token — about two dozen tokens a second — before any arithmetic is considered at all. The tensor cores are not the constraint. They are waiting.

That single division is the whole shape of the problem, and it is why batching is not an optimisation but the business model. The weights are read once per forward pass regardless of how many sequences are being advanced in it, so the per-token cost of the weights divides by the batch size. One user at a time wastes almost all of the hardware.

Which is where the key-value cache comes in, and where the second constraint bites. To avoid recomputing attention over the whole prefix for every new token, a serving engine keeps each session's past keys and values resident. That is a strictly good trade against recomputation, and it means every concurrent sequence holds memory proportional to its context length. Batching demands concurrency, concurrency demands resident caches, and the caches compete with the weights for the same 80GB. When the memory is gone, the server cannot admit a new request — it does not slow down, it refuses.

So memory management became the discipline of the field. Kwon and colleagues reported at SOSP 2023 that existing serving systems waste 60% to 80% of memory to fragmentation and over-reservation, with only 20.4% to 38.2% of allocated key-value memory holding actual token states in the layouts and workloads they profiled. Their system, vLLM, improves throughput by two to four times at the same level of latency against FasterTransformer and Orca, with the gain more pronounced for longer sequences, larger models and more complex decoding.

Note where that speedup came from, because it is the punchline. Not from faster mathematics. PagedAttention applies the idea of operating-system virtual memory to the cache: logically contiguous keys and values are stored in non-contiguous physical memory, each sequence's cache partitioned into blocks holding a fixed number of tokens, sixteen by default. A larger block lets the kernel process more positions in parallel and raises utilisation, at the price of more fragmentation. Two to four times more throughput, obtained by wasting less memory — which is a result about allocation, and a decades-old idea rediscovered because the bottleneck had moved.

problem.name: The bandwidth bound
problem.shape: A model must produce tokens one at a time, and each one requires reading the weights.
tell: hardware was chosen by arithmetic throughput and the observed rate is far below it
single-stream generation is slow and adding concurrent users barely slows it further
the server refuses new sessions rather than degrading
long contexts reduce the number of users who fit
problem.move: Compute the bandwidth floor before anything else: model bytes divided by memory bandwidth is the time per token for one stream. Then treat batch size as the lever that amortises it, and treat resident key-value cache as the thing that limits the batch — so memory efficiency, not arithmetic, is where the throughput is.
problem.invariant: Decoding one token of a dense model requires every parameter to cross the memory bus once, so time per token cannot fall below model bytes divided by bandwidth, however fast the arithmetic units are.
problem.breaks: The bound is for dense models decoding one token per pass. Anything that breaks either premise moves it — a mixture of experts reads only the routed parameters, speculative decoding produces several tokens per verification pass, and quantisation reduces the bytes directly. The arithmetic stays the same; the numerator changes.

cost.time: a batch is assembled before it runs, so throughput is bought with a small latency penalty for the first token
cost.space: every concurrent sequence holds keys and values for its whole context, and that memory competes with the weights on the same device
cost.beats: serving one request at a time, which is simplest and wastes nearly all of the hardware, and recomputing attention over the prefix each step, which frees the memory and squares the work

worked.problem: What is the difference between the prefill phase and the decode phase in serving, and why does one bind on compute while the other binds on memory bandwidth?
worked.reasoning:
They differ in how much work is available per pass over the weights, and that ratio decides which resource runs out first.

Prefill processes the whole input prompt at once. Every prompt token can be handled in parallel, so a single pass over the weights does a large amount of arithmetic — the matrices are big, the tensor cores are saturated, and the pass is compute-bound. The weights were read once and a great deal was done with them.

Decode generates one token per pass. The same weights are read again, and this time the arithmetic is a single position's worth. Almost nothing is done with the data that was just moved, so the cost is dominated by moving it: the phase is memory-bandwidth bound.

The arithmetic makes the asymmetry concrete. For a dense model at sixteen bits, two bytes per parameter, a seventy-billion-parameter model requires a hundred and forty gigabytes to cross the bus for one token. On hardware with 3.35TB/s of bandwidth that is roughly forty-two milliseconds, or about two dozen tokens a second, before considering the mathematics at all. The tensor cores are idle waiting for weights, and no amount of additional arithmetic throughput improves it.

Which yields the fix, and it is the reason batching is not an optimisation but the economics of serving. The weights are read once per pass regardless of how many sequences that pass advances, so the per-token weight cost divides by the batch size. Serving one user at a time is not merely inefficient; it wastes nearly all of the hardware, and the difference between a viable deployment and an unviable one is mostly whether the batch stays full. Continuous batching — admitting and retiring sequences as they arrive and finish rather than running fixed batches to completion — exists to keep it full.

And the second constraint follows immediately. Batching needs concurrency; concurrency needs each session's keys and values resident, so attention is not recomputed over the whole prefix every step; and those caches compete with the weights for the same device memory. So the limit on batch size, and therefore on throughput, is memory rather than arithmetic. When it runs out the server does not get slower — it refuses new sessions, which is a different failure mode from overload and needs a different response.

That is why the significant work in this area is allocation work. Kwon and colleagues reported that existing systems waste sixty to eighty per cent of memory to fragmentation and over-reservation, with only about a fifth to two fifths of allocated key-value memory holding real token states. Their system improves throughput by two to four times at the same latency, with larger gains for longer sequences and bigger models. The mechanism is operating-system virtual memory applied to the cache: logically contiguous keys and values placed in non-contiguous physical memory, each sequence partitioned into fixed-size blocks. Throughput multiplied by wasting less memory rather than by computing faster.

One boundary on all of the above, since the bound is often quoted too broadly. It assumes a dense model producing one token per pass. A mixture of experts reads only the routed parameters, speculative decoding yields several tokens per verification pass, and quantisation reduces the bytes outright. The division is unchanged — bytes over bandwidth — but each of those changes the numerator, which is exactly why they are the techniques the field pursues.

problem.practice: Work out the bandwidth floor for a model and device you have access to: parameters times bytes per parameter, divided by the device's memory bandwidth. Then measure single-stream tokens per second and compare. If the measurement is close to the floor, no amount of arithmetic throughput will help you, and every improvement has to come from the numerator or from the batch.

beats.broke: Serving was reasoned about as computation, so hardware was sized by arithmetic throughput — and decoding turned out to be limited by how fast weights can be moved rather than how fast they can be multiplied.
beats.fix: Read the bound off the bandwidth: one token of a dense model requires every parameter to cross the memory bus once, so time per token is model bytes over bandwidth — and the only fix is to amortise that crossing over a batch.
beats.cost: Amortising the weights over a batch requires the keys and values of every concurrent sequence to be resident at once, so memory rather than arithmetic sets the concurrency limit — and running out of it means refusing traffic rather than slowing down.

interview.q: What is the difference between the prefill phase and the decode phase in serving, and why does one bind on compute while the other binds on memory bandwidth?
interview.trap: Treating the request as computationally uniform. The two phases pass over the same weights and differ only in how much arithmetic is available per pass, which is precisely what decides which resource saturates.
interview.answer:
They differ in how much work is available per pass over the weights, and that ratio decides which resource runs out first.

Prefill processes the whole prompt at once. Every prompt token is handled in parallel, so one pass over the weights performs a large amount of arithmetic — big matrices, saturated tensor cores, compute-bound. The weights were read once and a great deal was done with them.

The arithmetic is concrete. At sixteen bits, two bytes per parameter, a seventy-billion-parameter dense model needs a hundred and forty gigabytes across the bus for one token. The tensor cores are waiting, and extra arithmetic throughput buys nothing.

So batching is the economics rather than an optimisation: the weights are read once per pass regardless of how many sequences it advances, so the per-token weight cost divides by the batch size, and serving one user at a time wastes nearly all of the hardware. The second constraint follows. So memory sets the batch size and therefore the throughput — and when it runs out the server refuses new sessions rather than slowing down, which is a different failure mode from overload.

That is why the important work is allocation. One boundary, because the bound gets quoted too broadly: it assumes a dense model producing one token per pass. A mixture of experts reads only the routed parameters, speculative decoding yields several tokens per verification pass, and quantisation cuts the bytes. The division is the same — bytes over bandwidth — but each changes the numerator, which is why they are the techniques the field pursues.
